content: German Chamomile, scientifically known as Matricaria recutita, is an annual plant belonging to the sunflower family, Asteraceae. It is also referred to as Chamomile and has several synonyms, including Chamomilla chamomilla, Chamomilla recutita (the accepted name according to Flora Europaea), Matricaria chamomilla, and Matricaria suaveolens. This plant typically grows in areas near human habitation across Europe and temperate regions of Asia. It has also been widely introduced to temperate areas of North America and Australia. Since its seeds require open soil to thrive, German Chamomile is often found growing along roadsides, near landfills, and in cultivated fields as a weed. Other common names for this plant include Wild Chamomile, Hungarian Chamomile, and Scented Mayweed. The plant features a branched, erect, and smooth stem that grows to a height of 15–60 cm. Its leaves are long, narrow, and either bipinnate or tripinnate in structure. The flowers are arranged in panicle-like capitula, with white ray florets that have ligules and yellow disc florets. The receptacle of the flower is hollow, swollen, and lacks scales, which distinguishes German Chamomile from Corn Chamomile (Anthemis arvensis), whose receptacle contains scales. The flowers emit a strong, aromatic fragrance and typically bloom from early to mid-summer. Medicinal Uses German Chamomile is widely used in herbal medicine for its therapeutic properties. It is commonly employed to alleviate conditions such as sore stomach, irritable bowel syndrome, and as a mild sleep aid. It is often consumed as an herbal tea, prepared by steeping two teaspoons of dried flowers per cup of tea. For individuals with a sore stomach, it is sometimes recommended to drink a cup of chamomile tea every morning on an empty stomach for two to three months. Additionally, it is used as a mouthwash to treat oral mucositis. German Chamomile also exhibits acaricidal properties, particularly against certain mites like Psoroptes cuniculi. The primary active ingredient in its essential oil is bisabolol, while other active compounds include chamazulene, flavonoids, and coumarins. Beyond its medicinal applications, chamomile is used cosmetically, most notably as a rinse to enhance the appearance of blonde hair. Agricultural Uses In agriculture, German Chamomile is sometimes referred to as the plant doctor due to its perceived ability to promote the growth and health of other plants, particularly those that produce essential oils. It is believed to enhance the production of these oils, thereby intensifying the scent and flavor of certain herbs, such as spearmint, sage, oregano, and basil. Chamomile tea is also thought to suppress fungal growth; for instance, misting it over seedlings may help prevent damping-off disease. However, German Chamomile can also act as an invasive species in agricultural fields. Farmers often need to manage its spread to maintain the productivity of their crops.
